subject: physics

items.q: Treat the Earth's surface as an inertial reference frame. Which of the following is also an inertial reference frame?
items.correct: A train on a straight, level track at a steady 30 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: A car going round a circular roundabout at a steady 30 m s⁻¹
items.why:
In everyday language 'speed' and 'velocity' are used interchangeably, and a speedometer reading that does not change feels like 'steady' motion. At GCSE many motion problems are in a straight line, where constant speed and constant velocity are the same thing. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a vector. A change of direction at constant speed is an acceleration (centripetal acceleration v²/r in uniform circular motion). A frame moving in a circle is therefore not inertial: in it, bodies with no resultant force on them do not move in straight lines.

Working: Inertial frame = non-accelerating. Train: straight track, constant speed → constant velocity, a = 0. Roundabout: direction changes, a = v²/r ≠ 0. Reversing lift: v = 0 momentarily but Δv/Δt ≠ 0. Rocket: a = 3 m s⁻² ≠ 0.
items.specStatementText: reference frames
items.random_wrong: A lift at the instant it is at rest while reversing direction
items.working: Inertial frame = non-accelerating. Train: straight track, constant speed → constant velocity, a = 0. Roundabout: direction changes, a = v²/r ≠ 0. Reversing lift: v = 0 momentarily but Δv/Δt ≠ 0. Rocket: a = 3 m s⁻² ≠ 0.

items.q: A passenger on a train moving at constant velocity says that the platform is moving backwards at 20 m s⁻¹. A person standing on the platform says that the train is moving forwards at 20 m s⁻¹. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Both are correct: each describes the motion relative to their own inertial frame.
items.misconception: Only the platform observer is correct, because the ground is the frame truly at rest.
items.why:
Everyday experience describes motion relative to the ground, and phrases such as 'the trees seemed to rush past' present the passenger's view as an illusion. The ground also feels fixed because we live on it. The ground is itself moving relative to the Sun and the Sun relative to the galaxy. Galilean and special relativity both state that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, so no experiment can pick out a frame that is 'really' at rest. Each observer's measurements are correct for their own frame.

Working: Train frame: platform velocity −20 m s⁻¹. Platform frame: train velocity +20 m s⁻¹. Both frames are inertial (constant velocity), so both descriptions are valid.
items.specStatementText: reference frames
items.random_wrong: Only the platform observer is correct, as a moving frame cannot be inertial.
items.working: Train frame: platform velocity −20 m s⁻¹. Platform frame: train velocity +20 m s⁻¹. Both frames are inertial (constant velocity), so both descriptions are valid.

items.q: A passenger in a train moving along a straight track at constant velocity drops a ball from rest relative to the train. Where does the ball land, and why?
items.correct: Directly below the point of release, as it keeps the train's horizontal velocity.
items.misconception: Behind the point of release, as the floor moves on while the ball is falling.
items.why:
Students hold the intuitive belief that motion needs a continuing push: once released, the ball is no longer carried by the train, so it should lose its forward motion. This 'impetus' idea is one of the most widely reported beliefs in research on intuitive mechanics. No horizontal force acts on the ball after release, so by Newton's first law its horizontal velocity stays equal to the train's. In the train's frame it falls straight down; this is Galilean relativity: mechanics experiments in a frame moving at constant velocity give the same results as at rest.

Working: Train frame: horizontal velocity 0, falls vertically, lands below release point. Platform frame: horizontal velocity = train's velocity, parabolic path; lands at the point that is then below the release point.
items.specStatementText: that Newton's laws of motion are the same in all inertial reference frames and this is known as Galilean relativity
items.random_wrong: Directly below the point of release, as the air in the carriage carries it.
items.working: Train frame: horizontal velocity 0, falls vertically, lands below release point. Platform frame: horizontal velocity = train's velocity, parabolic path; lands at the point that is then below the release point.

items.q: Observers in two inertial frames, S and S′, which move at a constant velocity relative to each other, both study a puck that is being pushed across ice and is accelerating. Which quantity do they measure to have the same value?
items.correct: The acceleration of the puck at any instant
items.misconception: The velocity of the puck at any given instant
items.why:
In most problems velocity is measured relative to the ground without saying so, so the frame is invisible and velocity seems to be a property of the object alone. Velocity is always velocity relative to a frame. Observers moving relative to each other measure different velocities for the same object; they agree on its acceleration when their relative velocity is constant.

Working: Galilean: u′ = u − v, v constant → a′ = Δu′/Δt = Δu/Δt = a. Velocity, momentum and position differ between the frames.
items.specStatementText: that Newton's laws of motion are the same in all inertial reference frames and this is known as Galilean relativity
items.random_wrong: The linear momentum of the puck at any instant
items.working: Galilean: u′ = u − v, v constant → a′ = Δu′/Δt = Δu/Δt = a. Velocity, momentum and position differ between the frames.

items.q: A ball rolls along a platform at 5.0 m s⁻¹. Frame S is the platform; frame S′ is a train moving at 25 m s⁻¹ in the positive x-direction relative to the platform. The origins of S and S′ coincide at t = 0. At t = 12 s the ball is at x = 450 m in S. What is the ball's position x′ in S′ at that instant?
items.why:
Students associate forward motion with increasing numbers and do not picture the origin of S′ moving towards the event. The same sign slip occurs when they write the inverse transformation. Draw both origins: at t = 0 they coincide; at time t the origin of S′ is at x = vt in S. The distance from the S′ origin to an event at x is x − vt. The inverse is x = x′ + vt.

Working: x′ = x − vt = 450 m − (25 m s⁻¹ × 12 s) = 450 m − 300 m = 150 m. (The ball's own speed of 5.0 m s⁻¹ is not needed.)
items.specStatementText: that in Galilean relativity the position x′ and time t′ of an event are given by x′ = x − vt and t′ = t
items.working: x′ = x − vt = 450 m − (25 m s⁻¹ × 12 s) = 450 m − 300 m = 150 m. (The ball's own speed of 5.0 m s⁻¹ is not needed.)

items.q: In Galilean relativity the time of an event in frame S′ is related to its time in frame S by t′ = t. What does this equation state?
items.correct: Both observers give each event the same time, whatever their relative motion.
items.misconception: Each observer gives a later time to an event the further away from them it happens.
items.why:
In everyday life we date events by when we see or hear them, and many popular accounts of relativity describe observers 'seeing' events. Research on students learning relativity repeatedly finds this belief, even after instruction. Each inertial frame is imagined filled with synchronized clocks; an event's time is read on the clock where it happens. Relativity of simultaneity remains after all signal delays are corrected: it comes from the t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) transformation, not from light travel time.

Working: t′ = t for all events → identical time coordinates, intervals and simultaneity in every inertial frame (absolute time).
items.specStatementText: that in Galilean relativity the position x′ and time t′ of an event are given by x′ = x − vt and t′ = t
items.random_wrong: The moving observer's clock runs slow, so it gives a smaller time to each event.
items.working: t′ = t for all events → identical time coordinates, intervals and simultaneity in every inertial frame (absolute time).

items.q: On a straight road, car A travels east at 35 m s⁻¹ and car B travels west at 22 m s⁻¹, both relative to the road. Take east as the positive direction. What is the velocity of car B in the reference frame of car A?
items.correct: −57 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: +57 m s⁻¹
items.why:
The phrase 'relative to' is easy to read backwards, and many students remember only that relative velocity involves 'a subtraction', not which way round. In u′ = u − v, u is the velocity of the object being observed and v is the velocity of the observer's frame. Computing v − u gives the velocity of A relative to B: the same size, opposite sign.

Working: u = −22 m s⁻¹ (B, road frame), v = +35 m s⁻¹ (A relative to road). u′ = u − v = −22 − 35 = −57 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that Galilean transformation equations lead to the velocity addition equation as given by u′ = u − v
items.random_wrong: −13 m s⁻¹
items.working: u = −22 m s⁻¹ (B, road frame), v = +35 m s⁻¹ (A relative to road). u′ = u − v = −22 − 35 = −57 m s⁻¹.

items.q: A spacecraft moves directly away from a laser at 0.50c relative to the laser. Applying u′ = u − v, an observer on the spacecraft should measure the laser light passing at 0.50c. Experiments of this kind find c for every inertial observer. What should be concluded?
items.correct: u′ = u − v is only an approximation, valid when speeds are much less than c.
items.misconception: The experiments must contain an error, since u′ = u − v is common sense.
items.why:
The equation matches all everyday experience and is taught first as the rule for relative velocity. It follows from the Galilean assumption that time is absolute, which feels self-evident. Experiments show that light has the same speed c for all inertial observers, which u′ = u − v cannot reproduce. The exact rule is the relativistic one, u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²), which reduces to u′ = u − v when u and v are much less than c.

Working: Galilean prediction in spacecraft frame: u′ = c − 0.50c = 0.50c. Measured: c. The Galilean equation is therefore only an approximation; special relativity replaces it.
items.specStatementText: that Galilean transformation equations lead to the velocity addition equation as given by u′ = u − v
items.random_wrong: Light is an exception as it is massless; u′ = u − v holds for massive bodies.
items.working: Galilean prediction in spacecraft frame: u′ = c − 0.50c = 0.50c. Measured: c. The Galilean equation is therefore only an approximation; special relativity replaces it.

items.q: Which statement is one of the two postulates of special relativity?
items.correct: The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.
items.misconception: No object with mass can reach or exceed the speed of light in a vacuum.
items.why:
'Nothing can go faster than light' is the best-known statement about relativity in popular science, so students assume it must be one of the starting assumptions. The second postulate is about the invariance of c. The speed limit follows from the theory: for example γ becomes infinite as v approaches c, and the relativistic velocity addition equation never gives a result greater than c.

Working: Postulate 1: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. Postulate 2: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.
items.specStatementText: the two postulates of special relativity
items.random_wrong: Light travels at the same speed in every medium it passes through.
items.working: Postulate 1: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. Postulate 2: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.

items.q: A spacecraft travels directly towards a distant star at 0.60c relative to the star. An astronaut measures the speed of the starlight arriving at the spacecraft. What does the astronaut find?
items.correct: c, as the speed of light in a vacuum does not depend on the motion of the observer
items.misconception: c, but only as the star is at rest; light from a moving star would be faster
items.why:
This is how thrown objects behave: a ball thrown from a moving car travels faster relative to the ground. Students extend the rule to light. Light is not launched like a ball. The second postulate, supported by experiment, states that c is independent of the motion of the source and of the observer. A moving source changes the frequency and wavelength (the Doppler effect), not the speed.

Working: Second postulate: the speed of light in a vacuum = c for all inertial observers. Neither Galilean addition (c + 0.60c = 1.6c) nor subtraction of speeds (c − 0.60c = 0.40c) applies; the astronaut measures c.
items.specStatementText: the two postulates of special relativity
items.random_wrong: 1.6c, as the speed of the spacecraft towards the star adds to the speed of light
items.working: Second postulate: the speed of light in a vacuum = c for all inertial observers. Neither Galilean addition (c + 0.60c = 1.6c) nor subtraction of speeds (c − 0.60c = 0.40c) applies; the astronaut measures c.

items.q: Frame S′ moves at v = 0.80c in the positive x-direction relative to frame S, and the origins coincide at t = t′ = 0. An event occurs at x = 900 m, t = 1.0 μs in S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the position x′ of the event in S′?
items.why:
Students recognise the Galilean part x − vt inside the bracket and, working quickly, apply only the familiar part of the formula, treating γ as a small correction. Both Lorentz equations are multiplied by γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Evaluate γ first from the given v, then multiply the whole bracket by it.

Working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.64) = 1/0.600 = 1.667. vt = (0.80)(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s) = 240 m. x′ = γ(x − vt) = 1.667 × (900 − 240) m = 1.667 × 660 m = 1100 m = 1.1 × 10³ m.
items.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)

items.q: Frame S′ moves at v = 0.80c in the positive x-direction relative to frame S, and the origins coincide at t = t′ = 0. An event occurs at x = 900 m, t = 1.0 μs in S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the time t′ of the event in S′?
items.why:
Everyday experience never shows a difference (at everyday speeds γ differs from 1 by less than one part in 10¹¹), and Galilean relativity, taught first, builds absolute time into t′ = t. Absolute time is an assumption of Galilean relativity that experiment contradicts at speeds near c. Muons moving at 0.995c survive about ten times longer in the Earth frame than at rest, exactly as Δt = γΔt₀ predicts. Only the space–time interval, not Δt alone, is the same for all observers.

Working: γ = 1.667. vx/c² = (0.80 × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ × 900 m)/(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)² = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ s. t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) = 1.667 × (1.0 × 10⁻⁶ − 2.4 × 10⁻⁶) s = 1.667 × (−1.4 × 10⁻⁶ s) = −2.33 × 10⁻⁶ s ≈ −2.3 μs.
items.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)

items.q: Which statement about the Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) is correct?
items.correct: It is never less than 1, and it increases without limit as v approaches c.
items.misconception: It is never greater than 1, and it decreases towards zero as v approaches c.
items.why:
Length contraction is often written L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²), so students meet the square-root expression without the reciprocal and attach the symbol γ to it; the idea that relativity makes things "smaller" makes a factor below 1 seem natural. γ is the reciprocal. Check γ = 1 at v = 0 and γ = 1.25 at 0.60c; any value below 1 means the expression is upside down.

Working: γ(0) = 1; γ(0.50c) = 1/√0.75 = 1.15; γ(0.87c) ≈ 2.0; γ → ∞ as v → c. Depends on v², so direction does not matter.
items.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
items.random_wrong: It increases in direct proportion to v, so it equals 2 when v is half of c.
items.working: γ(0) = 1; γ(0.50c) = 1/√0.75 = 1.15; γ(0.87c) ≈ 2.0; γ → ∞ as v → c. Depends on v², so direction does not matter.

items.q: In the Earth's frame S, spacecraft A moves at +0.60c and spacecraft B moves at −0.50c along the same line, towards each other. Frame S′ is the rest frame of A. Using u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²), what is the velocity of B in S′?
items.why:
Students substitute signed values into the numerator, where subtraction is familiar, but treat the uv/c² term as a magnitude, or mix the formula with a version written for addition. Substitute the signed velocities into every term. A useful check: the magnitude of the result must not exceed c. At high speeds this sign error can give a speed greater than c, which is a clear warning sign; at lower speeds it gives a wrong answer that looks reasonable, so always substitute the signs.

Working: u = −0.50c, v = +0.60c. uv/c² = (−0.50)(0.60) = −0.30. u′ = (−0.50 − 0.60)c/(1 − (−0.30)) = −1.10c/1.30 = −0.846c ≈ −0.85c.
items.specStatementText: that Lorentz transformation equations lead to the relativistic velocity addition equation as given by u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²)

items.q: An aircraft flies at 250 m s⁻¹ relative to the ground and a faster jet flies in the same direction at 800 m s⁻¹. A student compares u′ = u − v = 550 m s⁻¹ for the jet in the aircraft's frame with the relativistic value from u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²). Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Which evaluation is correct?
items.correct: uv/c² ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹², so the Galilean value differs from the relativistic one by a negligible amount.
items.misconception: The relativistic equation cannot be used, as relativity applies only to speeds near c.
items.why:
Textbooks introduce relativity with examples near c and say that at low speeds 'Newtonian physics works', which students read as a boundary between two domains rather than an approximation. The relativistic equations are valid at every speed. When u, v ≪ c the extra terms are tiny (for example uv/c² ≈ 10⁻¹² for aircraft), so they reduce to the Galilean equations to extremely high accuracy.

Working: uv/c² = (800 m s⁻¹)(250 m s⁻¹)/(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)² = 2.0 × 10⁵/9.0 × 10¹⁶ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹². Relativistic u′ = 550/(1 − 2.2 × 10⁻¹²) m s⁻¹ = 550 m s⁻¹ + 1.2 × 10⁻⁹ m s⁻¹. (Dividing by c only: 2.0 × 10⁵/3.00 × 10⁸ = 6.7 × 10⁻⁴.)
items.specStatementText: that Lorentz transformation equations lead to the relativistic velocity addition equation as given by u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²)
items.random_wrong: u − v is exact at these speeds, so the relativistic equation gives a slightly wrong value.

items.q: Two inertial observers in relative motion measure the same two events. Which quantity do they necessarily agree on?
items.correct: The quantity (cΔt)² − (Δx)², the square of the space–time interval between the events
items.misconception: The distance Δx between the two events, as distances do not depend on the frame
items.why:
Students learn that 'motion is relative' in terms of velocities, but think of positions as marks on a fixed background. They also confuse the separation of two events with the length of an object, which in Galilean relativity is the same in every frame. Position is measured from each frame's own origin, and the origins move apart. A ball thrown and caught on a moving train travels a short distance in the train frame but a long distance in the ground frame. Only the distance between two SIMULTANEOUS events (such as the two ends of an object) is the same in every Galilean frame.

Working: Invariant: (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)². Δt and Δx individually depend on the frame.
items.specStatementText: that the space–time interval Δs between two events is an invariant quantity as given by (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)²
items.random_wrong: The time interval Δt between the events, as time passes at an equal rate for every observer
items.working: Invariant: (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)². Δt and Δx individually depend on the frame.

items.q: In frame S, two events occur at the same place, 5.0 μs apart. In frame S′, which moves relative to S, the two events are 1200 m apart. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the time interval between the events in S′?
items.correct: 6.4 μs
items.misconception: 3.0 μs
items.why:
Students have used Pythagoras' theorem for every distance on a graph since early secondary school, and a space–time diagram looks like an ordinary graph drawn on paper. Space–time geometry is not Euclidean. The invariant combination is (cΔt)² − (Δx)². Consequences: the axes of a moving frame close up towards the 45° line instead of rotating rigidly, and their scales differ from those of the rest frame.

Working: S: cΔt = (3.00 × 10⁸)(5.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 1500 m, Δx = 0 → (Δs)² = 2.25 × 10⁶ m². S′: (cΔt′)² = (Δs)² + (Δx′)² = 2.25 × 10⁶ + 1.44 × 10⁶ = 3.69 × 10⁶ m² → cΔt′ = 1921 m → Δt′ = 1921/(3.00 × 10⁸) s = 6.4 × 10⁻⁶ s. (5.0 μs is the proper time, the shortest.)
items.specStatementText: that the space–time interval Δs between two events is an invariant quantity as given by (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)²
items.random_wrong: 9.0 μs

items.q: A muon is created in the upper atmosphere and later decays, moving at 0.99c relative to the Earth throughout. Which observer measures the proper time interval between its creation and its decay?
items.correct: An observer moving with the muon, as both events occur at the same place in that frame
items.misconception: Any observer with an accurate clock, as proper time means the correct time
items.why:
In everyday English 'proper' means correct or official, so students treat the proper time as the true value and other measurements as errors. All inertial observers' measurements are equally correct for their own frames. The proper time interval is special because it is measured in the one frame where both events happen at the same place; it is the shortest interval between those events.

Working: Proper time: frame in which both events occur at the same place → muon rest frame.
items.specStatementText: proper time interval and proper length
items.random_wrong: An observer at rest on the Earth, as the Earth is the frame that is not moving
items.working: Proper time: frame in which both events occur at the same place → muon rest frame.

items.q: An astronaut measures the length of her spacecraft. An observer on Earth, relative to whom the spacecraft moves at 0.60c along its length, also measures it. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The astronaut measures the proper length, the longest length found by any inertial observer.
items.misconception: The astronaut measures the proper length, the shortest length found by any inertial observer.
items.why:
Students learn proper time first, as the shortest time, and assume 'proper' quantities behave alike, especially as both are defined using the rest frame. The proper time interval is the shortest time; the proper length is the longest length. Check with the equations: Δt = γΔt₀ ≥ Δt₀ but L = L₀/γ ≤ L₀.

Working: Proper length L₀: measured in the rest frame of the object (astronaut). Earth: L = L₀/γ = L₀/1.25 = 0.80L₀.
items.specStatementText: proper time interval and proper length
items.random_wrong: The Earth observer measures the proper length, as the Earth is the frame that is truly at rest.
items.working: Proper length L₀: measured in the rest frame of the object (astronaut). Earth: L = L₀/γ = L₀/1.25 = 0.80L₀.

items.q: A spacecraft passes the Earth at 0.80c. A lamp on the spacecraft flashes once every 6.00 min, measured by a clock on the spacecraft. Earth observers time the flashes using clocks at rest in the Earth's frame. What time interval between flashes do they measure?
items.correct: 10.0 min
items.misconception: 3.60 min
items.why:
Students remember that 'moving clocks run slow' but mix up whose clock is slow and whose interval is longer, and the word 'dilation' is not tied to a particular frame. Identify the proper time first: it is measured in the frame where both events happen at the same place (the clock's own frame). The other frame measures γ times that, a longer interval, which is what 'the moving clock runs slow' means.

Working: Δt₀ = 6.00 min (spacecraft clock at both flashes). γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1/√0.36 = 1.667. Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.667 × 6.00 min = 10.0 min.
items.specStatementText: time dilation as given by Δt = γΔt₀
items.random_wrong: 16.7 min
items.working: Δt₀ = 6.00 min (spacecraft clock at both flashes). γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1/√0.36 = 1.667. Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.667 × 6.00 min = 10.0 min.

items.q: Spacecraft A and B pass each other at a relative speed of 0.60c. Each carries an identical clock. The astronaut in A says that B's clock runs slow, and the astronaut in B says that A's clock runs slow. Which evaluation is correct?
items.correct: Both are correct: each measures the clock moving relative to them to run slow, by γ = 1.25.
items.misconception: Neither is correct: the clocks only appear slow because light from them takes time to arrive.
items.why:
Popular explanations often mention light signals and what an observer 'sees', and everyday experience of delays (thunder after lightning) makes a signal-delay explanation feel natural. In special relativity the time of an event is recorded by a clock at that event, so signal delay has already been removed. The measured intervals and lengths are still different. Muons really do survive longer in the Earth frame, as counts at different altitudes show.

Working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1/0.80 = 1.25. Each frame measures the other's clock interval as Δt = 1.25Δt₀.
items.specStatementText: time dilation as given by Δt = γΔt₀
items.random_wrong: Only one can be correct: the clock that is really moving is the one that runs slow.
items.working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1/0.80 = 1.25. Each frame measures the other's clock interval as Δt = 1.25Δt₀.

items.q: A spacecraft has a proper length of 60.0 m. It moves past a space station at 0.60c along its length. What length does an observer on the space station measure for the spacecraft?
items.why:
Students learn time dilation first, where the moving frame's interval is multiplied by γ, and expect lengths to be multiplied in the same way. Time dilation multiplies the proper time by γ, but length contraction divides the proper length by γ. The two are consistent: a muon covers less distance in its own frame (contracted atmosphere) in less time (proper time).

Working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.36) = 1/0.80 = 1.25. L = L₀/γ = 60 m/1.25 = 48 m.
items.specStatementText: length contraction as given by L = L₀/γ

items.q: A lamp at the exact centre of a railway carriage flashes once. The carriage moves at constant high speed past a platform. In the carriage frame, the light reaches the front and rear doors at the same time. According to an observer on the platform, what happens?
items.correct: The light reaches the rear door first, as the rear door moves towards the light.
items.misconception: Both at once, as events simultaneous in one frame are simultaneous in every frame.
items.why:
Everyday life and Galilean relativity (t′ = t) both assume a universal time, and the belief feels too basic to question. In special relativity each frame has its own time coordinate. For two events simultaneous in S and separated by Δx, Δt′ = −γvΔx/c², which is zero only if Δx = 0 or v = 0.

Working: Platform frame: both pulses at c; rear door approaches its pulse, front door recedes from its pulse → rear door reached first.
items.specStatementText: the relativity of simultaneity
items.random_wrong: Both at once, as light going forwards moves at c + v and backwards at c − v.
items.working: Platform frame: both pulses at c; rear door approaches its pulse, front door recedes from its pulse → rear door reached first.

items.q: Two events are simultaneous in frame S and are 1200 m apart along the x-axis. Frame S′ moves at 0.60c along the x-axis relative to S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the time interval between the events in S′?
items.correct: 3.0 μs
items.misconception: 1.9 μs
items.why:
Students remember length contraction, L = L₀/γ, as 'relativity divides by γ' and transfer it to other equations without attending to their form. Each relativistic equation has its own place for γ: the Lorentz transformation multiplies by γ, time dilation multiplies the proper time by γ, and length contraction divides the proper length by γ. Use the equation as given.

Working: Δt′ = γ(Δt − vΔx/c²), Δt = 0. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.36) = 1.25. vΔx/c² = (0.60 × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)(1200 m)/(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)² = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ s. |Δt′| = 1.25 × 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ s = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ s.
items.specStatementText: the relativity of simultaneity
items.random_wrong: 2.4 μs

items.q: A space–time diagram for frame S has x on the horizontal axis and ct on the vertical axis, with equal scales. Which describes the world lines of a particle at rest in S and of a light pulse?
items.correct: Particle: a line parallel to the ct axis. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
items.misconception: Particle: a single point on the x axis of the diagram. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
items.why:
Students read a space–time diagram as a picture of where the object goes in space, so an object that goes nowhere has no line. A space–time diagram shows position against time. Even an object at rest exists at every instant, so it has an event at every value of ct: a vertical line through its fixed x.

Working: At rest: x constant → line parallel to ct axis. Light: Δx = cΔt = Δ(ct) → 45°.
items.specStatementText: space–time diagrams
items.random_wrong: Particle: a line parallel to the x axis. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
items.working: At rest: x constant → line parallel to ct axis. Light: Δx = cΔt = Δ(ct) → 45°.

items.q: A space–time diagram for frame S (axes x and ct) also shows the axes x′ and ct′ of a frame S′ moving relative to S. How are the scales on the ct′ and x′ axes determined?
items.correct: They are set by lines of constant space–time interval, so their units differ from those on ct and x.
items.misconception: They are identical to the scales on ct and x, because all four axes are measured in metres.
items.why:
On ordinary graphs, axes in the same unit share one scale, and students expect this convention to carry over. Having the same unit does not give the same drawn scale. On S's diagram, one unit on the ct′ axis is where the hyperbola (ct)² − x² = 1 crosses it, which is further from the origin than one unit on the ct axis.

Working: Scale on ct′: where (ct)² − x² = 1 crosses the ct′ axis (x = βct), ct = γ and x = βγ, so the distance from the origin on S's diagram is γ√(1 + β²) = √((1 + β²)/(1 − β²)) > 1. By symmetry, x² − (ct)² = 1 crosses the x′ axis at the same distance. Both primed units are longer than the unprimed units by the same factor.
items.specStatementText: space–time diagrams
items.random_wrong: They are shrunk by γ, because moving clocks run slow and moving lengths are contracted.
items.working: Scale on ct′: where (ct)² − x² = 1 crosses the ct′ axis (x = βct), ct = γ and x = βγ, so the distance from the origin on S's diagram is γ√(1 + β²) = √((1 + β²)/(1 − β²)) > 1. By symmetry, x² − (ct)² = 1 crosses the x′ axis at the same distance. Both primed units are longer than the unprimed units by the same factor.

items.q: A space–time diagram for frame S has axes x and ct in light-years (ly). Frame S′ moves at 0.50c along +x; its ct′ axis and x′ axis are each tilted by the same angle towards the 45° line, the x′ axis rising 0.50 ly of ct for each 1 ly of x. Event P is at (x = 0, ct = 2.0 ly) and event Q at (x = 4.0 ly, ct = 2.0 ly). What is the order of P and Q in S′?
items.correct: Q occurs before P, as Q lies below the line through P parallel to the x′ axis.
items.misconception: P occurs before Q, because Q lies further along the x′ axis, which tilts upwards.
items.why:
The sign of the vx/c² term is easy to reverse, and on a space–time diagram students often read the upward tilt of the x′ axis the wrong way. Use t′ = γ(t − vx/c²): for equal t, larger x gives smaller t′. On a space–time diagram, draw a line through one event parallel to the x′ axis: events below that line happen earlier in S′.

Working: x′-axis slope: Δ(ct)/Δx = v/c = 0.50. Line through P parallel to x′: ct = 2.0 + 0.50x → at x = 4.0 ly, ct = 4.0 ly. Q (ct = 2.0 ly) lies below → earlier in S′. Lorentz: γ = 1.155; cΔt′ = γ(0 − 0.50 × 4.0 ly) = −2.3 ly.
items.specStatementText: space–time diagrams
items.random_wrong: P and Q are simultaneous, because they lie on one line parallel to the x axis of S.
items.working: x′-axis slope: Δ(ct)/Δx = v/c = 0.50. Line through P parallel to x′: ct = 2.0 + 0.50x → at x = 4.0 ly, ct = 4.0 ly. Q (ct = 2.0 ly) lies below → earlier in S′. Lorentz: γ = 1.155; cΔt′ = γ(0 − 0.50 × 4.0 ly) = −2.3 ly.

items.q: On a space–time diagram with axes x and ct, the world line of a particle moving at constant velocity makes an angle of 25° with the ct axis. What is the speed of the particle?
items.why:
Students associate angles with resolving vectors into components, where sine and cosine are used, and choose a trigonometric function by habit. The two sides of the triangle are Δx (opposite θ) and Δ(ct) (adjacent to θ). Opposite over adjacent is tan θ, and Δx/(cΔt) = v/c.

Working: v = c tan θ = c tan 25° = 0.466c ≈ 0.47c.
items.specStatementText: that the angle between the world line of a moving particle and the time axis on a space–time diagram is related to the particle’s speed as given by tan θ = v/c
items.working: v = c tan θ = c tan 25° = 0.466c ≈ 0.47c.

items.q: A student draws the world line of an electron moving at constant velocity as a straight line at 50° to the ct axis. Which evaluation is correct?
items.correct: It cannot be correct: tan 50° ≈ 1.2, so the electron would have to move faster than light.
items.misconception: It cannot be correct: a line at more than 45° would mean that the electron moves back in time.
items.why:
Popular science links faster-than-light travel with time travel, and students repeat the connection without reading the diagram. For θ > 45°, tan θ > 1, so v > c. The line still rises in ct, so it does not go backwards in time; it is simply not a possible world line for a particle with mass.

Working: v/c = tan 50° = 1.19 > 1 → impossible for a massive particle. (tan 40° = 0.84; sin 50° = 0.77 are the errors.)
items.specStatementText: that the angle between the world line of a moving particle and the time axis on a space–time diagram is related to the particle’s speed as given by tan θ = v/c
items.random_wrong: It is possible: the angle to the x axis is 40°, so its speed is c tan 40° ≈ 0.84c.
items.working: v/c = tan 50° = 1.19 > 1 → impossible for a massive particle. (tan 40° = 0.84; sin 50° = 0.77 are the errors.)

items.q: Muons are produced 4.5 km above the ground (measured in the Earth's frame) and travel straight down at 0.995c. What is the thickness of this 4.5 km layer of atmosphere in the muons' rest frame?
items.why:
Students think of the muon as 'the thing that moves' and the Earth as fixed, so they attach every relativistic effect to the muon and assign the atmosphere's contraction to the wrong observer. Length contraction applies to any object moving relative to the observer. In the muons' frame the atmosphere moves, so it is contracted; in the Earth frame it is at rest, so it has its proper length and the muons' half-life is dilated instead.

Working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.995²) = 1/√0.009975 = 10.0. Proper length (Earth frame) L₀ = 4500 m. Muon frame: L = L₀/γ = 4500 m/10.0 = 449 m ≈ 4.5 × 10² m.
items.specStatementText: that muon decay experiments provide experimental evidence for time dilation and length contraction.
items.working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.995²) = 1/√0.009975 = 10.0. Proper length (Earth frame) L₀ = 4500 m. Muon frame: L = L₀/γ = 4500 m/10.0 = 449 m ≈ 4.5 × 10² m.

items.q: In a simplified muon experiment, muons moving at 0.995c (γ = 10.0) are counted at 1000 per hour by a detector on a mountain. An identical detector 2.25 km lower counts about 700 per hour. The muon half-life at rest is 1.5 μs, and the descent takes 7.5 μs in the Earth's frame. Which conclusion do the data support?
items.correct: Time dilation: in the Earth frame the half-life is about 15 μs, so about 700 per hour should arrive.
items.misconception: Time dilation: in the muons' own frame their half-life is dilated to 15 μs, so most survive.
items.why:
Popular accounts say that 'time slows down for a moving object', which students read as the moving object feeling time pass slowly in its own frame. Nobody feels their own time slow down: in its own frame a muon is at rest and has its normal half-life. In the muons' frame they survive because the atmosphere is contracted; in the Earth frame they survive because their half-life is dilated.

Working: Earth frame: descent time = 2250 m/(0.995 × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) = 7.5 μs. Dilated half-life = 10.0 × 1.5 μs = 15 μs → 0.50 half-lives → 1000 × 2^(−0.50) = 7.1 × 10² per hour ≈ observed 700. No dilation: 7.5/1.5 = 5.0 half-lives → 1000 × 2^(−5.0) ≈ 31 per hour. Muon frame: drop contracted to 2250/10.0 = 225 m, crossed in 0.75 μs = 0.50 half-lives → same prediction.
items.specStatementText: that muon decay experiments provide experimental evidence for time dilation and length contraction.
items.random_wrong: Length contraction: Earth observers measure the 2.25 km drop contracted to about 225 m.
items.working: Earth frame: descent time = 2250 m/(0.995 × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) = 7.5 μs. Dilated half-life = 10.0 × 1.5 μs = 15 μs → 0.50 half-lives → 1000 × 2^(−0.50) = 7.1 × 10² per hour ≈ observed 700. No dilation: 7.5/1.5 = 5.0 half-lives → 1000 × 2^(−5.0) ≈ 31 per hour. Muon frame: drop contracted to 2250/10.0 = 225 m, crossed in 0.75 μs = 0.50 half-lives → same prediction.

items.q: A cube has edges of proper length 2.0 m. It moves at 0.80c relative to an observer, parallel to one of its edges. Which statement gives the dimensions of the cube as measured by this observer?
items.correct: Its edge along the motion is 1.2 m; its other two edges are 2.0 m each.
items.misconception: All three of its edges are 1.2 m, because every dimension contracts by γ.
items.why:
The effect is usually introduced with a rod or spacecraft whose only interesting dimension lies along the motion, and everyday language ('moving objects shrink') carries no direction. Studies of students' reasoning about special relativity report that many apply the contraction to every dimension of the object. Length contraction is L = L₀/γ for the length along the direction of relative motion only. Perpendicular lengths are invariant, which can be checked directly: two identical rulers passing each other at right angles to their motion would each have to be shorter than the other if perpendicular lengths changed, a contradiction. A moving cube is therefore measured as a rectangular block, shortened along the motion only.

Working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1/√0.36 = 1/0.60 = 1.67.
Only the edge parallel to the relative velocity is contracted: L = L₀/γ = 2.0 m × 0.60 = 1.2 m.
The two edges perpendicular to the motion are unchanged at 2.0 m. The observer measures a block 1.2 m × 2.0 m × 2.0 m.
items.specStatementText: length contraction as given by L = L₀/γ
items.random_wrong: Its edge along the motion is 3.3 m; its other two edges are still 2.0 m each.
items.working:
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1/√0.36 = 1/0.60 = 1.67.
Only the edge parallel to the relative velocity is contracted: L = L₀/γ = 2.0 m × 0.60 = 1.2 m.
The two edges perpendicular to the motion are unchanged at 2.0 m. The observer measures a block 1.2 m × 2.0 m × 2.0 m.

items.q: Is a lift that is momentarily at rest, as it reverses from moving up to moving down, an inertial frame at that instant?
items.correct: No. Its velocity is zero only for an instant but it is changing, so its acceleration is not zero; it is not an inertial frame.
items.misconception: A frame that is at rest, even for an instant, has no acceleration, so it is an inertial frame at that moment.
items.why: Students link acceleration to how fast something is moving rather than to how fast its velocity is changing. The same belief makes them say that a ball at the top of its flight has zero acceleration. Acceleration is Δv/Δt, not v. A body whose velocity passes through zero while changing (a ball at the top of its flight, a lift reversing) has a non-zero acceleration at that instant. An inertial frame needs zero acceleration, not zero velocity.
items.specStatementText: reference frames
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a rocket moving with a constant (uniform) acceleration an inertial reference frame?
items.correct: No. An inertial frame has zero acceleration. A constant non-zero acceleration still changes the velocity, so the frame is not inertial.
items.misconception: A frame whose motion is 'uniform', including one with a uniform acceleration, is steady and therefore inertial.
items.why: The words 'uniform' and 'constant' are used both for constant velocity ('uniform motion') and for constant acceleration ('uniformly accelerated motion'), so students attach the idea of steadiness to the wrong quantity. Only a frame with constant velocity (zero acceleration) is inertial. In a uniformly accelerating rocket a released object does not stay at rest relative to the rocket: it appears to accelerate backwards, so Newton's first law does not hold in that frame.
items.specStatementText: reference frames
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must an inertial reference frame be at rest?
items.correct: No. An inertial frame may be at rest or moving with constant velocity; what matters is that it is not accelerating.
items.misconception: An inertial frame is one that is at rest; a moving frame cannot be inertial.
items.why: The word 'inertia' is associated in everyday use with staying still ('inertia' as reluctance to move), and the first examples students meet of Newton's first law are objects at rest. Newton's first law treats rest and constant velocity alike, and so does the definition of an inertial frame: a frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is itself inertial. Rest is simply the special case of constant velocity equal to zero.
items.specStatementText: reference frames
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a dropped ball keep up with a moving train because the air in the carriage carries it along?
items.correct: No. The ball keeps up because it already shares the train's velocity and no horizontal force changes it; it would do the same in a vacuum.
items.misconception: Objects inside a moving vehicle keep up with it only because the air inside is moving with the vehicle and carries them along.
items.why: Students know that wind pushes objects, and they notice that the air inside a car or train moves with it. It seems natural to credit the air with keeping things moving, which also fits the belief that motion needs a continuing push. Air resistance on a falling ball is small and would, if anything, only oppose motion relative to the air. The ball's horizontal velocity is unchanged because there is no horizontal resultant force (Newton's first law). The same result would hold in a vacuum: in a train carriage with the air removed, the dropped ball would still land directly below the point of release.
items.specStatementText: that Newton's laws of motion are the same in all inertial reference frames and this is known as Galilean relativity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a conserved quantity such as momentum have the same value in every inertial frame?
items.correct: No. Momentum is conserved within each frame, but its value depends on the frame because velocity does. Conserved means unchanged in time for an isolated system; invariant means the same in every frame.
items.misconception: If a quantity such as momentum or kinetic energy is conserved, all observers must measure the same value for it.
items.why: The words 'conserved', 'constant' and 'the same' are used loosely in everyday speech and in some textbooks, so 'stays the same during a collision' is heard as 'is the same for everyone'. Because velocities differ between frames (u′ = u − v), momentum mu and kinetic energy ½mu² differ too. Galilean relativity says the LAWS are the same in every inertial frame, so each observer finds momentum conserved, but with different numerical values. Acceleration and force are the quantities that are the same in all inertial frames in Galilean relativity.
items.specStatementText: that Newton's laws of motion are the same in all inertial reference frames and this is known as Galilean relativity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In x′ = x − vt, what does v represent?
items.correct: v is the velocity of frame S′ relative to frame S. It is not the velocity of any object whose position is being transformed.
items.misconception: The v in the transformation is the velocity of the moving object or event, so it is the object's speed that is multiplied by t.
items.why: In kinematics v almost always means the velocity of the object being studied, so students carry that habit into transformation equations where v means something else. The transformation converts coordinates between two frames, so the only velocity in it is the relative velocity of the frames. The object's own velocity enters only when it is itself being transformed, through u′ = u − v.
items.specStatementText: that in Galilean relativity the position x′ and time t′ of an event are given by x′ = x − vt and t′ = t
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the Galilean transformation include any slowing of moving clocks?
items.correct: No. In Galilean relativity t′ = t: time is absolute and every observer's clock agrees. Time dilation belongs to special relativity.
items.misconception: Even in Galilean relativity, a moving observer's clock runs slow, so t′ is smaller than t.
items.why: Students meet Galilean and special relativity in the same topic, often after hearing popular accounts of moving clocks running slow, and do not keep the assumptions of the two models separate. Galilean relativity assumes t′ = t for every event, so all intervals and simultaneity are the same for all inertial observers. That assumption is exactly what special relativity replaces; experiments at speeds near c, such as muon decay, show it fails.
items.specStatementText: that in Galilean relativity the position x′ and time t′ of an event are given by x′ = x − vt and t′ = t
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When two bodies move in opposite directions, can their speeds simply be subtracted to find the relative velocity?
items.correct: No. Velocities must carry signs. A velocity in the negative direction is negative, so for opposite directions u − v combines the two magnitudes.
items.misconception: Relative velocity is found by subtracting the smaller speed from the larger one, whatever the directions of motion.
items.why: Students learn 'relative velocity = difference' from examples where both bodies move the same way, and they work with speeds (magnitudes) rather than signed velocities. Choose a positive direction and give every velocity a sign before substituting. For bodies approaching each other at 35 m s⁻¹ and 22 m s⁻¹, the relative speed is 57 m s⁻¹, not 13 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that Galilean transformation equations lead to the velocity addition equation as given by u′ = u − v
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is light an exception to Galilean velocity addition only because it has no mass, with the rule still exact for massive objects?
items.correct: No. The Galilean rule fails for any object moving at a speed comparable to c, whether or not it has mass. Light shows the failure most clearly.
items.misconception: Light is a special case because it has no mass; for objects with mass the Galilean velocity addition equation is exact.
items.why: Students know that light is 'different' (massless, a wave) and look for a property of light to explain the anomaly, rather than questioning the assumption about space and time behind u′ = u − v. The failure comes from the Galilean assumption t′ = t, which applies to everything. For fast electrons or muons, u′ = u − v also gives wrong answers, and the relativistic equation gives the correct ones.
items.specStatementText: that Galilean transformation equations lead to the velocity addition equation as given by u′ = u − v
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the second postulate mean light travels at the same speed in every material?
items.correct: No. The postulate concerns the speed of light in a vacuum. In glass or water light travels more slowly than c.
items.misconception: The second postulate means that light travels at the same speed through every medium.
items.why: The postulate is often shortened to 'the speed of light is constant', dropping the words 'in a vacuum', and the same letter c is loosely used for the speed of light in air. The second postulate states that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers. Refraction exists precisely because light travels at different speeds in different media.
items.specStatementText: the two postulates of special relativity
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the time coordinate of an event in S′ simply γ times its time coordinate in S?
items.correct: No. t′ = γ(t − vx/c²). The term vx/c² depends on where the event happens and cannot be dropped unless x = 0.
items.misconception: Time in a moving frame is dilated, so the time coordinate of any event in S′ is t′ = γt.
items.why: Time dilation is the best-known result of special relativity, and students apply Δt = γΔt₀ to event coordinates instead of to a proper time interval. Δt = γΔt₀ relates time INTERVALS, and only when Δt₀ is a proper time interval. The time coordinate of a single event must be transformed with the full Lorentz equation, including the position-dependent term vx/c².
items.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does γ increase in proportion to v?
items.correct: No. γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) stays close to 1 for most of the range (γ = 1.15 at 0.50c) and rises steeply only as v approaches c.
items.misconception: γ increases in proportion to the speed, so it is 2 when v is half of c.
items.why: Students tend to assume linear relationships between quantities unless shown otherwise, and they rarely plot γ against v. Calculate γ at a few speeds: 1.00 at 0, 1.15 at 0.50c, 1.25 at 0.60c, 1.67 at 0.80c, 7.09 at 0.99c. The relationship is strongly non-linear, which is why relativistic effects are negligible at everyday speeds.
items.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is γ different for a frame moving towards an observer and one moving away?
items.correct: No. γ depends on v², so it has the same value whichever direction the relative motion is in.
items.misconception: Relativistic effects depend on whether the moving frame is approaching or receding, as the Doppler shift does, so γ (and the time dilation it gives) is different for approach and recession.
items.why: The Doppler effect, met earlier, does depend on whether a source approaches or recedes, and students expect every effect of relative motion to do the same. What an observer sees does depend on direction (an approaching clock is seen to tick fast, a receding one slow), because light travel time changes; the dilation measured after allowing for travel time depends only on speed. γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) contains only v², so it is the same for approach and recession, and it is never less than 1. Direction matters in the Lorentz transformation only through the sign of v in the brackets.
items.specStatementText: that the postulates of special relativity lead to the Lorentz transformation equations for the coordinates of an event in two inertial reference frames as given by x′ = γ(x − vt); t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) where γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In uv/c², is c squared?
items.correct: Yes. The term uv/c² is dimensionless only because c is squared: (m s⁻¹)(m s⁻¹)/(m s⁻¹)² has no unit.
items.misconception: The correction term is uv/c, so dividing by c once is enough.
items.why: Students evaluating a long expression with a calculator often enter c once instead of c², and do not check that the term is dimensionless. Check the units: uv has unit m² s⁻², so it must be divided by c² (m² s⁻²) to give a pure number that can be subtracted from 1. Dividing by c alone leaves a unit of m s⁻¹, which cannot be subtracted from 1.
items.specStatementText: that Lorentz transformation equations lead to the relativistic velocity addition equation as given by u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the interval be found as Δs = cΔt − Δx without squaring?
items.correct: No. The invariant is (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)². Only the squared combination has the same value in every frame.
items.misconception: The space–time interval is Δs = cΔt − Δx, so no squaring is needed.
items.why: Students remember that the interval 'is cΔt minus Δx' and drop the squares, much as they sometimes add vector magnitudes instead of using Pythagoras. Always write (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)² and take the square root at the end if Δs itself is needed. The unsquared difference cΔt − Δx is not the same in different frames.
items.specStatementText: that the space–time interval Δs between two events is an invariant quantity as given by (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is γ = 1/(1 − v²/c²)?
items.correct: No. γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Without the square root γ is far too large: at 0.80c the correct value is 1.67, not 2.78.
items.misconception: γ is 1/(1 − v²/c²), without a square root.
items.why: The square root sign covers the whole of 1 − v²/c² and is easily lost when copying the formula or entering it into a calculator. Evaluate 1 − v²/c² first, take its square root, then take the reciprocal. Check against known values: γ = 1.25 at 0.60c and 1.67 at 0.80c.
items.specStatementText: time dilation as given by Δt = γΔt₀
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²), is v/c squared?
items.correct: Yes. At 0.80c, v²/c² = 0.64 and γ = 1/√0.36 = 1.67. Using 0.80 instead of 0.64 gives γ = 2.24, which is wrong.
items.misconception: γ = 1/√(1 − v/c), so the ratio v/c is used without squaring.
items.why: When v is given as a fraction of c, students substitute the fraction directly and forget that the formula uses its square. Write β = v/c and compute β² before subtracting from 1. At 0.80c, β² = 0.64 and γ = 1/√0.36 = 1.67.
items.specStatementText: time dilation as given by Δt = γΔt₀

items.q: If each of two observers measures the other's clock to run slow, is that a contradiction?
items.correct: No. Each observer measures the clock that moves relative to them to run slow. The measurements concern different pairs of events, and simultaneity differs between the frames, so the results are consistent.
items.misconception: It cannot be true that each observer measures the other's clock to run slow; either one of them is wrong or the effects cancel so that neither clock really runs slow.
items.why: Everyday logic says that if A's clock is slower than B's, B's cannot be slower than A's. Students treat 'running slow' as an absolute property of a clock rather than a comparison made in a particular frame. Time dilation is reciprocal, as the first postulate requires: neither inertial frame is preferred. Each observer compares one moving clock with two separated, synchronized clocks of their own, and the relativity of simultaneity makes both results consistent.
items.specStatementText: time dilation as given by Δt = γΔt₀
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a space–time diagram read like a distance–time graph, with an object at rest shown as a horizontal line?
items.correct: No. On a space–time diagram ct is on the vertical axis and x on the horizontal, so an object at rest is a vertical line.
items.misconception: An object at rest has a horizontal world line, as on a distance–time graph.
items.why: In earlier courses motion graphs always have time on the horizontal axis, so students transfer the reading 'horizontal = at rest' without noticing the axes are swapped. Always check the axes: space–time diagrams in this course put x horizontal and ct vertical. A horizontal line joins events at the same time in different places; it is not the world line of any object.
items.specStatementText: space–time diagrams

items.q: Why is the world line of light at 45° rather than almost horizontal?
items.correct: Because the time axis is ct, not t. In a time Δt light travels cΔt, so Δx = Δ(ct) and the line is at 45°.
items.misconception: Light is so fast that its world line is horizontal: it travels any distance in no time.
items.why: On an ordinary x–t graph in SI units, light's line would be almost horizontal, and students are used to treating light as instantaneous in everyday problems. Plotting ct instead of t gives both axes the unit of length and makes the speed of light the 45° line. A horizontal line would mean infinite speed, which is impossible.
items.specStatementText: space–time diagrams
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the scales on the primed axes simply compressed by γ?
items.correct: No. The scale is set by the hyperbola of constant interval; as drawn on S's diagram, one unit on a primed axis is longer, not shorter, than on the unprimed axis.
items.misconception: The primed axes have their scales shrunk by γ, because moving clocks run slow and moving lengths contract.
items.why: Students apply the headline results of relativity (things 'shrink' and 'slow down') directly to the drawn diagram without using the invariant interval. Mark units using lines of constant space–time interval: (ct)² − x² = 1 unit² crosses the ct′ axis at ct′ = 1. Time dilation and length contraction then follow from the diagram; they are not built into the scale by hand.
items.specStatementText: space–time diagrams

items.q: In tan θ = v/c, from which axis is θ measured?
items.correct: From the ct (time) axis. θ = 0 for a particle at rest, whose world line is parallel to the ct axis.
items.misconception: θ is measured from the x axis, as the gradient angle is on an ordinary graph.
items.why: On distance–time graphs the angle a line makes with the horizontal (time) axis gives the speed, and students carry that habit over even though the time axis is now vertical. On a space–time diagram the time axis ct is vertical. A particle at rest has θ = 0 measured from it, and light has θ = 45°. Measuring from the x axis gives the complementary angle and tan of that equals c/v.
items.specStatementText: that the angle between the world line of a moving particle and the time axis on a space–time diagram is related to the particle’s speed as given by tan θ = v/c
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a particle's speed proportional to the angle its world line makes with the ct axis?
items.correct: No. v/c = tan θ, which is not proportional to θ: 22.5° corresponds to 0.41c, not 0.50c.
items.misconception: Since light is at 45°, speed is proportional to angle, so v = (θ/45°)c.
items.why: Students know the two fixed points (0° for rest, 45° for light) and interpolate linearly between them. tan θ is not linear in θ. Always use v = c tan θ; for example 25° gives 0.47c, not 0.56c.
items.specStatementText: that the angle between the world line of a moving particle and the time axis on a space–time diagram is related to the particle’s speed as given by tan θ = v/c

items.q: Does time dilation stretch the ct′ axis and length contraction shrink the x′ axis of a moving frame on a space–time diagram?
items.correct: No. Both primed scales are set by the invariant hyperbolae, and on S's diagram a unit on ct′ and a unit on x′ are both drawn longer than a unit on ct or x, by the same factor.
items.misconception: Time dilation stretches the time axis and length contraction shrinks the space axis of a moving frame, so on a space–time diagram the ct′ scale is stretched by γ and the x′ scale is shrunk by γ.
items.why: Students picture time dilation as time being 'stretched' and length contraction as lengths being 'squashed', and transfer these words directly to the scales of the drawn axes without using the invariant interval. Mark units with lines of constant space–time interval: (ct)² − x² = 1 crosses ct′ at ct′ = 1 and x² − (ct)² = 1 crosses x′ at x′ = 1. Both points lie at the same distance √((1 + v²/c²)/(1 − v²/c²)) from the origin on S's diagram, so the two primed scales are changed in the same way; time dilation and length contraction are then read off the diagram.
